old_observations.text: The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).

old_observations.text: How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.

old_observations.text: The given-or-taken line is stated outright. "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7): This is the plainest statement in the three batches of what the researcher suspected. Human pride holds as its own what was received; The researcher's word "assumed" fits: the standing is taken up as if it were not given; The right measure is the one God assigns. "not to think of himself more highly than he ought ... according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God has height by nature, a person has a measure by gift. Pride is thinking past the gift; Taking God's seat; "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); Together with Eze 28:2 and Isa 14:13 (batches 1–2), the verses show pride at its full height as a claim to God's own place; I read: God's "Most High" is the place pride reaches for. Batches 1–3 show no one holding it but God; Christ's firstness is grounded, and pleased; "that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Col 1:18–19); His first place rests on what he is: before all things, the one through whom all were made, firstborn from the dead. It is not claimed against anyone; Batch 1 also has Christ's majesty as "received ... from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17), and his seat taken "after making purification for sins" (Heb 1:3); I read: in the verses the Son's height comes with his descent: firstborn from the dead, seated after purification. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself; God's knowing is what pride meets. "God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God" (Luk 16:15). "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luk 1:51). As in batch 2 (1Sa 2:3), God's knowledge is joined to his answer to pride; Other beings in these verses (held, not read in); A messenger of Satan is given against conceit (2Co 12:7); The conceited may fall "into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6); Angels greater in might do not blaspheme where the willful do (2Pe 2:11); These are for 13.2 and 13.3. The verses do not say that the devil fell by pride. That is not stated here and is not built on.

old_observations.text: Corinthians 10–12 is one long passage in which Paul is forced to boast, and he turns the boast round: As a fool. "accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool" (2Co 11:16–17). He names the boast foolish while he makes it; Weakness. "If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness" (11:30). What follows is being let down a wall in a basket (11:32–33); Visions. "I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations" (12:1). Then "On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses" (12:5); No more than is seen. "if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me" (12:6); I read: this is the opposite of pride's assumed standing. He holds back even a true boast so that his standing in others' eyes is no higher than what is so; Power in weakness. "I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me ... For when I am weak, then I am strong" (12:9–10); Authority given. "if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you" (2Co 10:8). The authority is given, and it is given for others; "this boasting of mine will not be silenced": that he served them without burdening them (2Co 11:9–10).

old_observations.text: God is not the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object, and his character is what is boasted in. "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24). The proper boast is knowing God as he is: The boast is moved, not removed. The same impulse that boasts in wisdom, might and riches (Jer 9:23) is turned to God (9:24; 1Co 1:31). It becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3); I read: set beside batches 1–3, the human "lifting" is not abolished. Where it rests on oneself it is pride. Where it rests on God it is glory in him. This fits Ch 12 claim C-182 (the boast moved to what God does). It is a reconciliation point when that chapter is touched; Gift excludes self-boasting. "it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Eph 2:8–9). "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1Co 4:7). "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); This is the researcher's "assumed" in the verses' words: a standing held as one's own when it was received, or thought when it is not so; The contrast with God, from batches 1–3, is that his standing is neither received nor assumed; The measure is assigned. "the area of influence God assigned to us" (2Co 10:13), and in batch 3 "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God's height is his by nature, a person's rightful standing is a measure given, and pride boasts "beyond limits"; Christ's power in weakness. "my power is made perfect in weakness ... so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9). The boast in weakness makes room for another's power. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself, as in batch 3 §3.4; God's steadfast love answers the boast of evil. "Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day" (Psa 52:1). God's character is set over the mighty man's boast, as his mercy answered presumption in batch 2 §3.7.

old_observations.text: Where responsibility sits. The commands address the stages from lodging onward: "forsake … his thoughts" (Isa 55:7); "let none of you devise evil" (Zech 7:10); "take every thought captive" (2 Cor 10:5); "wash your heart" (Jer 4:14); The *arising* is not commanded, but it is not neutral either. What comes up shows the condition of the heart (Gen 6:5; Mark 7:21). So thoughts that arise reveal the heart, and devising engages the will. The heart itself can be changed from outside: written on, given discretion, guarded, or darkened.

old_observations.text: 3. New — not yet in any chapter: The path from thought to deed (§9.3). Arising (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Luk 24:38) → lodging (Jer 4:14) → reckoning (Isa 53:4) → devising (Ps 36:4) → expression through tongue, lips and eyes (Ps 52:2; Pro 16:30) → action through hand and feet (Mic 2:1; Pro 6:18; Isa 59:7). The same path runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59). Commands address the stages from lodging onward. Arising is not commanded, but it shows the state of the heart.; Thinking as reckoning, i.e. assigning worth (§9.2.2). Human misreckoning (Gen 38:15; 1Sa 1:13; Isa 53:3–4) against God's reckoning (Gen 15:6; Ps 32:2; Isa 40:15, 17). This links directly to justification language. It has no home in the narrative yet.; Thoughts that arrive, especially at night (§9.1.2–3). The bed is where thoughts come unbidden (Dan 2:29) and also where people plot on purpose (Ps 36:4; Mic 2:1). The night thoughts are tied to revelation (Dan 2:29–30).; Thought moves the body (§9.2.4). "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way" (Dan 5:6); the divided mind "limping between two different opinions" (1Ki 18:21). This fits Ch 6 (flesh) or Ch 11 §3 ("The parts give way in sequence").; Outbound hearing: God hears the plots (§13.1). "You have heard their taunts … all their plots" (Lam 3:61); Mal 3:16. The narrative has hearing only as the inbound way in. Your comment in the discussion: *"Yes, hearing is an integral part of the outbound thought."*; Design and craft as the good form of devising (§9.2.1). Exod 26:1; 35:32–35: God fills craftsmen with skill "to devise artistic designs".

existing_observations.text: The surface 'conceive' carries nine codes in two senses, with one rhetorical use between them. evidence.verse: thinking, “ If Esau comes to the one camp and attacks it, then the camp that is left will escape.”

And David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, “ lest they should tell about us and say, ‘ So David has done.’” Such was his custom all the while he lived in the country of the Philistines.
And Achish trusted David, thinking, “He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant.”

And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, “You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off”— thinking, “ David cannot come in here.”

And the king rose in the night and said to his servants, “I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the open country, thinking, ‘When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive and get into the city.’”
After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah and encamped against the fortified cities, thinking to win them for himself.
For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, “Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done.” But now, O God, strengthen my hands.
They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, “ Who can see them?”

senses.obs_text: In these eight verses the Hebrew verb of saying introduces a thought quoted as a sentence: Jacob, David, Achish, the Jebusites, the king of Israel, Sennacherib, Nehemiah's enemies and the wicked each 'say' it in themselves. The thought is inner speech, usually about what others will do or what will not be seen. Verses: Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2Ch 32:1, Neh 6:9, Psa 64:5.
senses.grounds: they talk of laying snares secretly

evidence.verse: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.”

though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more:

evidence.verse: “ And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words.
He said, “ Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “ What do you think, Simon? From whom do kings of the earth take toll or tax? From their sons or from others?”
What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray?
“ What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, ‘ Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’
Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?”
saying, “ What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.”
Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?
Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?”
Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division.
And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way?
Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem?
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,
Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.
They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “ What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”
They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.
For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty,
I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.

How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?

senses.obs_text: In these seven verses 'think' is a question put to a hearer for his view: 'What do you think?' asks Jesus, and the hearers are asked about a case, a person or a coming. It asks for a judgment the hearer already forms. Verses: Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56.
senses.grounds: What do you think about the Christ

senses.obs_text: In these verses 'think' is holding a belief, often one the verse then corrects: the Gentiles' belief that many words are heard, the belief that Jesus cannot appeal to his Father, that he came to give peace, that the Galileans were worse, that the Scriptures give life apart from him, that killing believers serves God. In the Pauline verses it is Paul's own estimate of the apostles' place, of his judgment, of the body's parts and of the foolish. Verses: Mat 6:7, Mat 26:53, Luk 12:51, Luk 13:2, Luk 13:4, Joh 5:39, Joh 5:45, Joh 16:2, 1Cor 4:9, 1Cor 7:40, 1Cor 12:23, 2Cor 11:16, Heb 10:29.
senses.grounds: Do you think that I cannot appeal

evidence.verse: To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be.

But as for me, this mystery has been revealed to me, not because of any wisdom that I have more than all the living, but in order that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your mind.

Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king answered and said, “ Belteshazzar, let not the dream or the interpretation alarm you.” Belteshazzar answered and said, “My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you and its interpretation for your enemies!
Then the king’s color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together.
The queen, because of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banqueting hall, and the queen declared, “O king, live forever! Let not your thoughts alarm you or your color change.

The same thoughts carry revelation in one place and fear in the others. Verses: Dan 2:29, Dan 2:30, Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10, Dan 7:28.
senses.grounds: his thoughts alarmed him

Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.

senses.grounds: they thought it was a ghost

senses.grounds: the Lord takes thought for me

evidence.verse: But lately my people have risen up as an enemy; you strip the rich robe from those who pass by trustingly with no thought of war.

senses.obs_text: In Mic 2:8 'with no thought of war' is the Hebrew verb of turning back from war: the trusting passers-by who are stripped have returned from fighting. Verses: Mic 2:8.
senses.grounds: with no thought of war

evidence.verse: For behold, he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought, who makes the morning darkness, and treads on the heights of the earth — the Lord, the God of hosts, is his name!

senses.obs_text: In Amo 4:13 'thought' is the Hebrew word for musing or meditation: God declares to man what his own thought is, as the maker of mountains and wind. Verses: Amo 4:13.
senses.grounds: declares to man what is his thought
